extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policy watchers interested in Twitter/X under Elon Musk
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of policies, enforcement decisions, product changes, and moderation standards implemented or altered at Twitter/X during Elon Musk's ownership. Covers content-moderation criteria, labeling/verification rules, API/monetization limits, and algorithmic promotion practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move to automation to restrict diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter moved towards more automation to moderate content, intended to restrict diffusion rather than outright removal; described by Musk as 'freedom of speech, not freedom of reach'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes automated limiting of content reach (demotion/visibility restrictions) as a primary enforcement mechanism; contrasts removal vs restricting amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-tolerance policy on 'violent speech' (Feb 28, 2023)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter adopted an updated zero-tolerance policy on 'violent speech' on February 28, 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The updated policy was described by reporting as simultaneously 'more specific and more vague' than the prior version; exact enforcement criteria were not always transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doxxing real-time location: suspension standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Any account doxxing real-time location information of anyone will be suspended, as it is considered a physical safety violation; posting slightly delayed location data is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy text (and Musk's statement) distinguishes between real-time location (suspend) and delayed-location posts (permitted); used to justify suspensions such as ElonJet and associated accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated, targeted harassment enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated, targeted harassment against any account will cause the harassing accounts to receive, at minimum, temporary suspensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harassment enforcement includes minimum temporary suspensions for repetition/targeting; context (e.g., who is targeted, severity) affects outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of 'cis'/'cisgender' as slurs (in context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter declared the words 'cis' or 'cisgender' are considered slurs on the platform within the context of repeated and targeted harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification applies when such words are used as part of repeated targeted harassment; not a blanket ban of the terms in all contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation/non-enforcement of misgendering/deadnaming rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Musk indicated a policy review that resulted in misgendering or deadnaming of transgender individuals not being enforced; earlier protections were effectively relaxed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content that previously would have been removed might instead remain, or receive lighter treatment (e.g., labels), reflecting a shift away from strict enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of warning labels instead of removals for potential hateful conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter announced it would place warning labels on tweets that are 'potentially' in violation of its hateful conduct policy, rather than removing them (April 2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts enforcement from content removal to labeling; may reduce takedowns while signaling potential policy concerns to users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of reporting tools for transphobic abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: At one point the ability to report allegations of transphobic abuse had been scrapped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural change reduced user-facing mechanisms for reporting certain categories of abuse, affecting enforcement throughput and data capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy rule: prohibition on disclosure of others' real names
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter amended its privacy policy to prohibit disclosure of others' real names (in response to doxxing incidents involving a pseudonymous user).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify suspending users who revealed alleged real names of pseudonymous individuals; broadened the platform's privacy/doxxing protections to include identity disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-affiliated / government-funded media labeling criteria (and changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter applied labels such as 'US state-affiliated media' and later 'government-funded' to accounts (e.g., NPR), sometimes relying on external lists (reportedly a Wikipedia category); labels and applied percentages (e.g., '70% government-funded') were adjusted or removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling criteria appear to have been applied inconsistently (examples include NPR, BBC, PBS, CBC), causing controversy and prompting reversals and eventual removal of the state-affiliated label for many outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification policy tied to paid subscription (Twitter Blue) and badge categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning November 2022, Twitter required users to purchase a Twitter Blue subscription to obtain verification; legacy verification badges were removed and new badges included gold checkmarks for businesses and gray checkmarks for government accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change was implemented amid impersonation concerns; the Trust and Safety team assessed impersonation risks and verification launches were paused or halted at times to address spikes in impersonation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Halting/removal of legacy verification badges
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter announced removal of legacy (pre-change) verification badges; only Twitter Blue subscribers would retain or receive the blue checkmark unless other badge categories applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legacy badges were removed in stages (announced dates moved); some notable users temporarily had blue checkmarks without paying, indicating operational inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: API monetization and restrictions on third-party clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter retroactively updated its developer agreement to bar developers from creating products similar to Twitter's own app, removed the free API tier and replaced it with paid tiers, and cut off many third-party clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy changes limited third-party application functionality and access, cited as a move to address data scraping and system manipulation; had downstream impacts on ecosystem tools and integrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading/viewing rate limits by account verification status
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary limits were applied to the number of posts an account could read per day: verified accounts limited to 6000 posts/day, unverified accounts 600/day, and new unverified accounts 300/day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits were framed as a response to extreme levels of data scraping and system manipulation; applied differently by account type and subject to later adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on unregistered users and DM sending limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter temporarily blocked unregistered users from viewing tweets or profiles and limited the number of direct messages unverified users could send per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures were presented as anti-bot/anti-abuse steps; they affected accessibility for casual or unregistered viewers and reduced friction for potential harassment vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid write/post access for new users (pilot program)
rubrics_metrics.description: X began charging new users in select countries an annual fee to use basic features such as posting, replying, and quoting (pilot programs like New Zealand and the Philippines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a means to curb bots and reduce automated abuse; this monetization approach ties posting privileges to payment for new entrants in some regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic 'For You' feed and paid-boosting mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's 'For You' tab shows an algorithmically curated feed similar to TikTok; with a paid Twitter Blue subscription, users can have their tweets boosted by the algorithm. Instances of algorithmic boosting (including promotion of Elon Musk's tweets by large factors) were reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic curation determines reach; paid boosts and manual algorithmic changes can materially alter visibility and were linked to shifts in content prominence and allegations of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of non-amplification policy for state-controlled media
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter reversed an earlier policy that would not recommend or amplify state-controlled media entities, allowing algorithmic promotion of accounts from state-controlled outlets (e.g., Russia's RT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change enabled greater reach for government-run media and was followed by rapid follower increases for those accounts; seen as a substantive shift in recommendation policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension standard for calls to extreme violence / implied genocide
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter stated that 'clear calls for extreme violence' are against the terms of service and will result in suspension; this standard was invoked for phrases it deemed implied genocide (e.g., 'decolonization', 'from the river to the sea').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of the standard involved interpretation of political/activist phrases as incitement; decisions were publicly debated and sometimes supported by outside groups (e.g., ADL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to block/mute features and compatibility with app store policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed deletion of the 'Block' feature (keeping it for DMs) and replacement with a stronger 'Mute' feature were announced; concerns were raised that removing block might violate App Store and Google Play policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature design choices must consider platform store policies and anti-bullying advocates; backlash influenced leadership statements and some feature confirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of user posts to train generative AI
rubrics_metrics.description: X announced that posts could be used to train generative AI regardless of individual user consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy change affects user data usage and privacy expectations; it has implications for consent, data rights, and public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account suspension/reinstatement practices (broad reinstatements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the takeover, many previously banned accounts (including far-right and extremist accounts) were reinstated; high-profile suspensions and reinstatements (journalists, activists) occurred frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinstatement decisions were sometimes rapid and applied to accounts previously removed for policy violations, reflecting a shift in enforcement philosophy and inconsistent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Notes as a crowd-sourced moderation signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Musk referenced the crowd-sourced Community Notes program as part of broader plans to address disinformation and content moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community Notes were presented as a non-platform-centric moderation input to inform user context and trust signals, though their efficacy and scale vary.
